O R D E R
1. Permission to file Special Leave Petition(s)
is granted.
2. Applications seeking impleadment/ intervention
are allowed.
3. Applications  seeking  addition/  deletion/
modification of parties are allowed.
4. Leave granted.
5. Challenge in this batch of appeals is to the
orders passed by the learned Single Judge and the
Full Bench of the Patna High Court on the same issue.
For the sake of convenience, we treat the appeals
arising out of the SLP(C) Nos. 10872-10898/2024 as
the lead case which arises out of the Full Bench
judgment of the Patna High Court. The Full Bench was
constituted as the matter was refereed to a larger
Bench noticing the controversy as to the acquisition

--- Page 313 ---
3
of  Diploma  in  Elementary  Education;  the  minimum
qualification for appointment of teachers in the
primary school as prescribed by the NCTE. Since,
there were divergence in opinion by different Benches
of the High Court, including the Single Judge and the
Division Bench, the Full Bench took up the matter so
as to give a quietus to the issue at the High Court
level.
6. In the present batch of appeals, there are
appellants who were appointed prior to 31.03.2015 and
thereafter also. The Full Bench, in the operative
part of the impugned judgment, passed the following
order/ directions:
“41. On the interpretation given by us to Section
23(1), we issue the following directions:-
 
(1) those who were appointed prior to 01.04.2010
who have acquired the teaching qualification on or
before  08.08.2021  would  be  entitled  to  be
continued;
(2) the results withheld, when declared, if it
relates back to the period before 08.08.2021,
those persons should be continued in employment;
 
(3) the issuance of certificates also would have
to concede to the date of publication of results;
which  if  published  before  08.08.2021,  those
persons will be deemed to have been continued;
(4) the unqualified teachers who were appointed
during  the  relaxation  period,  i.e.  between
01.04.2010 and 31.03.2015 will also be deemed to
have been continued, if they have acquired the
teachers  training  qualification;  the  minimum
qualification, on or before 08.08.2021.
(5)  The  persons,  who  were  appointed  after
31.03.2015, if are unqualified will have to be

--- Page 314 ---
4
terminated  even  if,  they  have  acquired  the
qualification  within  08.08.2021;  since  their
appointment itself is invalid. There could not
have been any unqualified persons appointed after
31.03.2015.
(6)  Those  who  were  in  place  as  teachers  on
01.04.2010 and then on 31.03.2015, if not acquired
the qualification before 08.08.2021 will stand
terminated.”
7. Insofar as the unqualified teachers appointed
after  31.03.2015  are  concerned,  since  their
appointment,  at  the  inception,  were  illegal  for
violating Section-23(1) of the Right of Children to
Free and Compulsory Education Act, 2009 (for short,
‘the RTE Act’), the Full Bench has rightly concluded
that their appointments cannot be saved by allowing
them to continue and acquire qualification within an
extended time frame.
8. Upon  hearing  learned  counsel  for  the
appellant(s), who are aggrieved by the dismissal of
their petitions/appeals by the High Court, we are in
agreement with the reasoning assigned and thus, such
appellants in the present batch of appeals, who were
appointed after 31.03.2015, have no case in their
favour and their appeals are dismissed.
9. In respect of such teachers, who were in
service on or before 31.03.2015, the High Court, by
the impugned judgment, has extended the time for
acquiring the qualification of Diploma in Elementary
Education (D.El.Ed) within 08.08.2021 and the said

--- Page 315 ---
5
batch of teachers have been allowed to continue in
service till they acquire such qualification on or
before 08.08.2021.
10. Mr. Vikas Singh and Mr. Santosh Kumar, learned
senior counsels and other learned counsel appearing
for  the  appellants,  who  were  in  service  on
31.03.2015, would submit that their case is covered
by judgments rendered by this Court in: (i) Anjuman
Ishaat-E-Taleem Trust Vs. State of Maharashtra and
Ors. (2025 SCC Online SC 1912) and (ii) State of U.P.
Vs. Anjuman Ishaat-E-Taleem Trust & Ors. (2026 SCC
online SC 998).
11. In the first judgment, Anjuman Ishaat-E-Taleem
Trust (supra),  this Court, while dealing with the
issue  of  acquiring  the  minimum  qualification  of
Teacher Eligibility Test (TET), directed that insofar
as  in  service  teachers  recruited  prior  to  the
enactment of the RTE Act, i.e. 31.03.2015, and having
more than 05 years to retire on superannuation are
concerned, they shall be under an obligation to
qualify  TET  within  two  years  from  the  date
(01.09.2025) on which the judgment was delivered, in
order to continue in service. If any of such teachers
fail to qualify the TET within the time granted by
this Court, they shall have to quit service. For the
sake of clarity, paragraph- 217 of the first Anjuman
Ishaat-E-Taleem Trust judgment (supra) is extracted

--- Page 316 ---
6
below:
“217. Insofar  as  in-service  teachers
recruited prior to enactment of the RTE Act
and having more than 5 years to retire on
superannuation are concerned, they shall be
under an obligation to qualify the TET within
2 years from date in order to continue in
service. If any of such teachers fail to
qualify the TET within the time that we have
allowed, they shall have to quit service.
They may be compulsorily retired; and paid
whatever terminal benefits they are entitled
to. We add a rider that to qualify for the
terminal benefits, such teachers must have
put in the qualifying period of service, in
accordance with the rules. If any teacher has
not put in the qualifying service and there
is  some  deficiency,  his/her  case  may  be
considered by the appropriate department in
the Government upon a representation being
made by him/her.”
12. Thereafter, in the second Anjuman Ishaat-E-
Taleem Trust (supra), the time allowed for acquiring
the TET qualification was extended by 31.08.2028 by
observing thus:
“32.  Having  regard  to  the  paramountcy  of
ensuring continuity in elementary education of
children, we deem it appropriate to grant
limited relief by extending the period earlier
stipulated  for  acquiring  the  TET
qualification, again, in exercise of our power
under Article 142 of the Constitution.
33. Appreciating that the TET examination must
be  conducted  by  the  relevant  authorities
expeditiously  as  well  as  the  time  and
resources required for the same are limited,
we alter and extend the timeline granted in
paragraph  217  of  Anjuman (supra)  for  in-
service  teachers  to  acquire  the  TET
qualification from 2 (two) to 3 (three) years,
i.e., the qualification has to be obtained by
31st August, 2028 instead of 31st August, 2027,
as originally directed.
34. Needless to observe, it shall also be the

--- Page 317 ---
7
endeavour of the respective States and the
competent  authorities  to  conduct  the  TET
periodically, and preferably twice every year,
interspersed with an approximate period of six
months between the successive examinations, so
as to afford eligible teachers a reasonable
opportunity  to  comply  with  the  statutory
requirement.
35.  We  make  it  abundantly  clear  that  no
further prayer for extension of time shall be
entertained.”
13. Although, learned counsel appearing for
the State of Bihar made efforts to distinguish the
judgments rendered by this Court in Anjuman Ishaat-E-
Taleem  Trust  (supra),  however,  after  sometime,
learned counsel agreed that like TET, D.El.Ed is also
an essential qualification.
14. In our considered view, since TET and
D.El.Ed  both  are  essential  qualification  for
appointment as teachers at the primary school level,
the direction contained in Anjuman Ishaat-E-Taleem
Trust can be applied in the present cases also.
15. There is no dispute that D.El.Ed is an
essential qualification and thus, once the appellants
were lacking in that qualification but, were in
service on 31.03.2015, the  time  extended  in
Anjuman Ishaat-E-Taleem Trust squarely applies for
them also and thus, we dispose of all such appeals in
which the appellants were in service on 31.03.2015,
allowing  them  time  to  acquire  the  D.El.ED

--- Page 318 ---
8
qualification  on  or  before  31.08.2028.  Those
candidates, who were appointed prior to 31.03.2015
but, have been terminated in terms of the High Court
order, shall be allowed to continue so that they are
given time to acquire the qualification on or before
31.08.2028. The result of D.El.Ed examination held
already shall be declared at the earliest.
16. We make it abundantly clear that no further
extension of time will be entertained.
17. The appeals are accordingly  disposed of, in
the above terms.

    (PRASHANT KUMAR MISHRA)

New Delhi

O R D E R
1. Permission to file Special Leave Petition(s)
is granted.
2. Applications seeking impleadment/ intervention
are allowed.
3. Applications  seeking  addition/  deletion/
modification of parties are allowed.
4. Leave granted.
5. Challenge in this batch of appeals is to the
orders passed by the learned Single Judge and the
Full Bench of the Patna High Court on the same issue.
For the sake of convenience, we treat the appeals
arising out of the SLP(C) Nos. 10872-10898/2024 as
the lead case which arises out of the Full Bench
judgment of the Patna High Court. The Full Bench was
constituted as the matter was refereed to a larger
Bench noticing the controversy as to the acquisition

--- Page 326 ---
3
of  Diploma  in  Elementary  Education;  the  minimum
qualification for appointment of teachers in the
primary school as prescribed by the NCTE. Since,
there were divergence in opinion by different Benches
of the High Court, including the Single Judge and the
Division Bench, the Full Bench took up the matter so
as to give a quietus to the issue at the High Court
level.
6. In the present batch of appeals, there are
appellants who were appointed prior to 31.03.2015 and
thereafter also. The Full Bench, in the operative
part of the impugned judgment, passed the following
order/ directions:
“41. On the interpretation given by us to Section
23(1), we issue the following directions:-
 
(1) those who were appointed prior to 01.04.2010
who have acquired the teaching qualification on or
before  08.08.2021  would  be  entitled  to  be
continued;
(2) the results withheld, when declared, if it
relates back to the period before 08.08.2021,
those persons should be continued in employment;
 
(3) the issuance of certificates also would have
to concede to the date of publication of results;
which  if  published  before  08.08.2021,  those
persons will be deemed to have been continued;
(4) the unqualified teachers who were appointed
during  the  relaxation  period,  i.e.  between
01.04.2010 and 31.03.2015 will also be deemed to
have been continued, if they have acquired the
teachers  training  qualification;  the  minimum
qualification, on or before 08.08.2021.
(5)  The  persons,  who  were  appointed  after
31.03.2015, if are unqualified will have to be

--- Page 327 ---
4
terminated  even  if,  they  have  acquired  the
qualification  within  08.08.2021;  since  their
appointment itself is invalid. There could not
have been any unqualified persons appointed after
31.03.2015.
(6)  Those  who  were  in  place  as  teachers  on
01.04.2010 and then on 31.03.2015, if not acquired
the qualification before 08.08.2021 will stand
terminated.”
7. Insofar as the unqualified teachers appointed
after  31.03.2015  are  concerned,  since  their
appointment,  at  the  inception,  were  illegal  for
violating Section-23(1) of the Right of Children to
Free and Compulsory Education Act, 2009 (for short,
‘the RTE Act’), the Full Bench has rightly concluded
that their appointments cannot be saved by allowing
them to continue and acquire qualification within an
extended time frame.
8. Upon  hearing  learned  counsel  for  the
appellant(s), who are aggrieved by the dismissal of
their petitions/appeals by the High Court, we are in
agreement with the reasoning assigned and thus, such
appellants in the present batch of appeals, who were
appointed after 31.03.2015, have no case in their
favour and their appeals are dismissed.
9. In respect of such teachers, who were in
service on or before 31.03.2015, the High Court, by
the impugned judgment, has extended the time for
acquiring the qualification of Diploma in Elementary
Education (D.El.Ed) within 08.08.2021 and the said

--- Page 328 ---
5
batch of teachers have been allowed to continue in
service till they acquire such qualification on or
before 08.08.2021.
10. Mr. Vikas Singh and Mr. Santosh Kumar, learned
senior counsels and other learned counsel appearing
for  the  appellants,  who  were  in  service  on
31.03.2015, would submit that their case is covered
by judgments rendered by this Court in: (i) Anjuman
Ishaat-E-Taleem Trust Vs. State of Maharashtra and
Ors. (2025 SCC Online SC 1912) and (ii) State of U.P.
Vs. Anjuman Ishaat-E-Taleem Trust & Ors. (2026 SCC
online SC 998).
11. In the first judgment, Anjuman Ishaat-E-Taleem
Trust (supra),  this Court, while dealing with the
issue  of  acquiring  the  minimum  qualification  of
Teacher Eligibility Test (TET), directed that insofar
as  in  service  teachers  recruited  prior  to  the
enactment of the RTE Act, i.e. 31.03.2015, and having
more than 05 years to retire on superannuation are
concerned, they shall be under an obligation to
qualify  TET  within  two  years  from  the  date
(01.09.2025) on which the judgment was delivered, in
order to continue in service. If any of such teachers
fail to qualify the TET within the time granted by
this Court, they shall have to quit service. For the
sake of clarity, paragraph- 217 of the first Anjuman
Ishaat-E-Taleem Trust judgment (supra) is extracted

--- Page 329 ---
6
below:
“217. Insofar  as  in-service  teachers
recruited prior to enactment of the RTE Act
and having more than 5 years to retire on
superannuation are concerned, they shall be
under an obligation to qualify the TET within
2 years from date in order to continue in
service. If any of such teachers fail to
qualify the TET within the time that we have
allowed, they shall have to quit service.
They may be compulsorily retired; and paid
whatever terminal benefits they are entitled
to. We add a rider that to qualify for the
terminal benefits, such teachers must have
put in the qualifying period of service, in
accordance with the rules. If any teacher has
not put in the qualifying service and there
is  some  deficiency,  his/her  case  may  be
considered by the appropriate department in
the Government upon a representation being
made by him/her.”
12. Thereafter, in the second Anjuman Ishaat-E-
Taleem Trust (supra), the time allowed for acquiring
the TET qualification was extended by 31.08.2028 by
observing thus:
“32.  Having  regard  to  the  paramountcy  of
ensuring continuity in elementary education of
children, we deem it appropriate to grant
limited relief by extending the period earlier
stipulated  for  acquiring  the  TET
qualification, again, in exercise of our power
under Article 142 of the Constitution.
33. Appreciating that the TET examination must
be  conducted  by  the  relevant  authorities
expeditiously  as  well  as  the  time  and
resources required for the same are limited,
we alter and extend the timeline granted in
paragraph  217  of  Anjuman (supra)  for  in-
service  teachers  to  acquire  the  TET
qualification from 2 (two) to 3 (three) years,
i.e., the qualification has to be obtained by
31st August, 2028 instead of 31st August, 2027,
as originally directed.
34. Needless to observe, it shall also be the

--- Page 330 ---
7
endeavour of the respective States and the
competent  authorities  to  conduct  the  TET
periodically, and preferably twice every year,
interspersed with an approximate period of six
months between the successive examinations, so
as to afford eligible teachers a reasonable
opportunity  to  comply  with  the  statutory
requirement.
35.  We  make  it  abundantly  clear  that  no
further prayer for extension of time shall be
entertained.”
13. Although, learned counsel appearing for
the State of Bihar made efforts to distinguish the
judgments rendered by this Court in Anjuman Ishaat-E-
Taleem  Trust  (supra),  however,  after  sometime,
learned counsel agreed that like TET, D.El.Ed is also
an essential qualification.
14. In our considered view, since TET and
D.El.Ed  both  are  essential  qualification  for
appointment as teachers at the primary school level,
the direction contained in Anjuman Ishaat-E-Taleem
Trust can be applied in the present cases also.
15. There is no dispute that D.El.Ed is an
essential qualification and thus, once the appellants
were lacking in that qualification but, were in
service on 31.03.2015, the  time  extended  in
Anjuman Ishaat-E-Taleem Trust squarely applies for
them also and thus, we dispose of all such appeals in
which the appellants were in service on 31.03.2015,
allowing  them  time  to  acquire  the  D.El.ED

--- Page 331 ---
8
qualification  on  or  before  31.08.2028.  Those
candidates, who were appointed prior to 31.03.2015
but, have been terminated in terms of the High Court
order, shall be allowed to continue so that they are
given time to acquire the qualification on or before
31.08.2028. The result of D.El.Ed examination held
already shall be declared at the earliest.
16. We make it abundantly clear that no further
extension of time will be entertained.
17. The appeals are accordingly  disposed of, in
the above terms.
.....................J.
    (PRASHANT KUMAR MISHRA)
....................J.
(SHREE CHANDRASHEKHAR)
New Delhi

IN THE SUPREME COURT OF INDIA 
CIVIL ORIGINAL JURISDICTION 
 
WRIT PETITION (CIVIL) NO(S). 758 OF 2025  
 
 
IN RE: ISSUES RELATING TO ECOLOGY AND 
ENVIRONMENTAL CONDITIONS PREVAILING IN 
THE STATE OF HIMACHAL PRADESH 
 
O R D E R 
 
1. The present proceedings were initiated suo motu 
by this Court in view of the recurring ecological 
degradation and environmental concerns confronting 
the State of Himachal Pradesh. Noticing that the 
issues involved transcended isolated incidents and 
called for a comprehensive examination of the factors 
contributing to the deterioration of the fragile 
Himalayan ecosystem, this Court directed the 
registration of the present writ petition. Considering 
the wide -ranging nature of the issues arising for 
consideration, this Court, by order dated  25th 
August, 2025, appointed Mr. K. Parmeshwar, learned 

--- Page 338 ---
2 
 
Senior Advocate, assisted by Ms. A akashi Lodha, 
Advocate-on-Record, as amicus curiae to assist the 
Court in the matter. 
2. Upon considering the detailed study and 
analysis undertaken by the learned amicus curiae, 
this Court, by order dated 23rd September, 2025, took 
on record the exhaustive questionnaire prepared by 
the learned amicus curiae, identifying the broad areas 
requiring examination, including zoning, forest and 
tree cover, compensatory afforestation, climate 
change, disaster management, road infrastructure, 
hydroelectric projects, mining and tourism. Being of 
the view that the respo nses to the aforesaid queries 
would provide the necessary factual foundation for 
evolving appropriate measures to protect the fragile 
ecology of the affected area, this Court directed the 
State of Himachal Pradesh to furnish its response, 
duly supported by an affidavit of the Principal 
Secretary, Department of Forest, before the next date 
of hearing. 
3. When the matter was taken up for hearing

                             O R D E R
The Court at the very outset record its utter displeasure at
the conduct of the respondent no.1, which is borne from our orders
recorded in the present proceedings. 
2. The  clear-cut  picture,  which  has  emerged  is  that  the
respondent no.1 to put it mildly, has tried to mislead the Court by
repeatedly coming up with proposals to clear the dues of the
petitioner  within  time  frames  fixed  and  even  the  Court
accommodating him and accepting the said request to the extent of
giving him time for six months for making the payments, not even
one commitment to the Court has been truthfully discharged. 
3. Learned counsel for the respondent no.1 tried to canvass the
issue that the petitioner has been coming up with different figures
at different points of time and the exact figure of how much the
respondent no.1 is required to pay to the petitioner, is still not
clear. 
4. In this also, we find that the lack of bonafide is writ large
on the part of the respondent no.1 inasmuch as, despite the record
showing that at least Rs.7,00,50,000/- (Rupees Seven Crores Fifty
Thousand) still remains to be paid by the respondent no.1, going
only by the principal amount, which is said to have been defalcated

--- Page 350 ---
3
by him belonging to the petitioner, today again, time is being
sought by the respondent no.1 of four weeks just to file an
affidavit  bringing  on  record  the  capacity/assets  which  the
respondent no.1 possesses. The Court would pause here to indicate
that on the one hand, there is a lis before a Court, which has to
be decided whereas, equally important is the fact that on the other
hand, a person/respondent no.1 is here, who is taking the Court
proceedings casually and has not been truthful and fair to the
Court. Thus, the Court is equally required/called upon to take a
view with regard to what has to be done so that people do not take
the Courts for granted and sanctity is maintained of the orders
which the Courts pass on the basis of trust as represented by the
parties concerned. 
5. In the present case, the respondent no.1 has been present in
Court in various proceedings and after consulting him and taking
instructions from him, learned counsel representing him had made
those commitments before this Court. The Court is not here to judge
whether the respondent no.1 is in a capacity to pay the amount or
not; fact remains that a commitment before the Court is sacrosanct
and has to be mandatorily complied with. 
6. In the aforesaid background, for the present, we find that the
respondent no.1 needs to be proceeded against strictly for such act
which is nothing short of committing contempt. Matters become
worse, as the said contempt is committed in the face of the Court
for the reason that a commitment was made personally before the
Court and the same was not complied with, not once but on several
occasions. Today, the Court has completely lost trust/faith in the

--- Page 351 ---
4
respondent  no.1’s  coming  out  truthfully  and  discharging  the
liability, which is cast upon him in law.
7. Thus, we find that for this conduct, the respondent no.1 is
required to be sent to Civil Prison with immediate effect.
8. After  the  order  was  dictated,  learned  counsel  for  the
respondent no.1, upon instructions from the respondent no.1, who is
present in the Court submitted that the matter may be listed at the
top of the Board on the reopening day of this Court i.e.,
immediately after partial court working days i.e., on 13.07.2026
and before that day, the respondent no.1 shall transfer an amount
of Rs.2,50,00,000/- (Rupees Two Crores Fifty Lakhs) in favour of
the petitioner.
9. Though, the Court is sceptical of the undertaking given by
respondent no.1, but because the matter has been vehemently pursued
by the learned counsel for the respondent no.1, who has assured the
Court that probably, this time the respondent no.1 would not fail,
acceding to the request, more as an indulgence to the learned
counsel than to the respondent no.1, the matter be listed at the
top of the Board on 13.07.2026, when an affidavit shall be filed by
the respondent no.1 before this Court bringing on record the
evidence showing transfer of the said amount in favour of the
petitioner. On the next date of listing, the respondent no.1 shall
also be personally present in the Court.
10. Till the next date of listing, the Court refrains from passing
appropriate orders on the basis of what has been recorded earlier,
relating to the conduct of the respondent no.1.

--- Page 352 ---
5
11. Learned senior counsel for the petitioner submitted that
though the payments being made by the respondent no.1 is being
deposited in a special account, but as per the Court’s order,
withdrawals are not permitted without express permission of this
Court and on the last occasion, an amount of Rs.25,00,000/- (Rupees
Twenty Five Lakhs) was allowed to be withdrawn by the petitioner,
keeping in mind the age and the health condition of the petitioner,
the Court may allow further withdrawal.
12. Having regard to the aforesaid, the Court permits withdrawal
of a further amount of Rs.25,00,000/- (Rupees Twenty Five Lakhs)
from the said corpus for the use of the petitioner.
13. Before parting, learned senior counsel for the petitioner
submitted that by way of assisting the Court, a clear-cut case for
proceeding against the respondent no.1 has also been made out in
terms of the law laid down by this Court in Subrata Roy Sahara v
Union of India and Others (2014) 8 SCC 470.

IN THE SUPREME COURT OF INDIA
CIVIL ORIGINAL JURISDICTION
WRIT PETITION (CIVIL) NO. 889 OF 2025
XXXX                   …PETITIONER(S)
                                VERSUS
INDIAN INSTITUTE OF TECHNOLOGY, 
KHARAGPUR & ORS.                …RESPONDENT(S)
O R D E R
This  writ  petition  has  been  filed  under  Article  32  of  the
Constitution of India seeking the following reliefs:
“In the premises aforesaid, it is most respectfully prayed
that this Hon’ble Court may be pleased to:
(i) Issue a writ of mandamus or any other appropriate writ,
order or direction directing the 1 st and 2 nd Respondents
to jointly and simultaneously  process the Petitioner’s
medical transfer application in strict accordance with
the  Inter-IIT  Transfer  Rules  within  a  period  of  two
weeks,  with  the  medical  board  being  constituted
exclusively at AIIMS Delhi or IIT Delhi to ensure access
to  specialized  mental  health  expertise,  impartial
evaluation free from institutional bias, and proximity to
the Petitioner’s required treatment facilities. 
(ii) Issue a writ of mandamus or any other appropriate writ,
order  or  direction  directing  the  2nd Respondent  (IIT
Delhi) to honour the conditional consent provided by its
Director on 27.12.2023 and admit the Petitioner to any
1

--- Page 369 ---
suitable undergraduate program of their choice, either
according to his rank or to the program in which the
lowest  ranked  student  was  admitted  in  the  relevant
academic  year,  contingent  upon  completion  of  the
medical  evaluation  process  mandated  in  prayer  (i)
above.
 
(iii) In the alternative, direct the 2 nd Respondent to create a
supernumerary seat for the Petitioner in any suitable
undergraduate  program  at  IIT  Delhi,  considering  his
exceptional  medical  circumstances,  meritorious
academic  record  (JEE  Advanced  AIR  3587),  and  the
urgent  necessity  for  geographical  proximity  to
specialized medical facilities at AIIMS Delhi and family
support system in Punjab; 
(iv) Pass any other order or direction as this Hon’ble Court
may deem fit and proper in the circumstances of the
case and in the interest of justice.” 
2. Briefly stated, the facts of the case are that in July 2023, the
petitioner commenced his studies in Bachelor of Architecture (B.Arch.)
course, Department of Architecture and Regional Planning at Indian
Institute of Technology (‘IIT’), Kharagpur, first-respondent herein. The
petitioner  is  stated  to  suffer  from  Borderline  Personality  Disorder
(‘BPD’),  whose  symptoms  resurfaced  post  his  admission  to  IIT,
Kharagpur. The petitioner has averred that a re-evaluation led to a
definitive diagnosis of BPD as a chronic condition, confirmed through
multiple medical consultations, including a re-assessment at PGIMER
Chandigarh. The petitioner has averred that his condition requires
Repetitive Transcranial Magnetic Stimulation (‘RTMS’) therapy, along
2

--- Page 370 ---
with continuous parental supervision. Further, while RTMS facilities
exist in West Bengal, they are located in Kolkata and not Kharagpur.
However, even the facilities in Kolkata are in prohibitively expensive
private hospitals beyond the petitioner’s financial means. Affordable
government facilities providing this treatment are available at AIIMS
Delhi, which is close to the campus of IIT, Delhi.
3. Therefore,  following  the  recurrence  of  severe  symptoms,  the
petitioner initiated a request for an inter-IIT transfer to IIT, Delhi in
November 2023. Since IIT, Delhi does not offer a B.Arch. course, the
petitioner  has  stated  that  the  transfer  would  have  necessitated  a
placement in a suitable Bachelor of Technology (‘B.Tech.’) course, or to
a  branch  to  which  the  lowest  All  India  Rank  JEE  student  was
admitted. However, by letter dated 13.02.2024 by the Chairman JEE
(Advanced), the request was formally rejected on four primary grounds
— insufficient JEE rank, curriculum differences, non-equivalency of
the B.Arch. and B.Tech. courses and inapplicability of the transfer
rules to Architecture students.
4. Subsequently, the petitioner sought legal aid through both the
Delhi  and  Calcutta  High  Court  Legal  Services  Committees.  Both
Committees’  panel  advocates  declined  jurisdiction.  Thereafter,  the
petitioner approached the National Legal Services Authority (‘NALSA’),
3

--- Page 371 ---
which  forwarded  the  matter  to  the  Supreme  Court  Legal  Services
Committee in April 2025. Hence, the present Writ Petition was filed,
inter  alia, seeking  directions  to  process  the  petitioner’s  medical
transfer application. The petitioner contends,  inter alia , that there is
demonstrable substantial course compatibility between the petitioner’s
B.Arch. program and the B.Tech. program at IIT, Delhi.
5. By  order  dated  26.09.2025,  this  Court  issued  notice  in  the
instant matter. By order dated 15.07.2026, this Court noted that the
petitioner cannot avail of a transfer to IIT, Delhi on medical grounds,
owing  to  the  difference  in  the  curriculum  of  the  B.Arch.  course.
Therefore, learned senior counsel, Ms. Shoba Gupta submitted that
the  petitioner  may  be  transferred  to  IIT,  Roorkee.  Recording  this
submission, this Court directed the petitioner to appear before AIIMS
Delhi  on  20.07.2026,  so  that  the  petitioner  would  be  medically
evaluated, and a report would be submitted to this Court by a Medical
Board constituted by the Director of AIIMS.
6. The Medical Board has submitted its report dated 23.07.2026, in
which it concluded that after a detailed assessment of the petitioner
and a review of previous medical records, the Board is of the opinion
that the petitioner “is suffering from recurrent depressive disorder and
is currently asymptomatic and maintaining well on medication”.
4

--- Page 372 ---
7. We  have  heard  learned  senior  counsel  for  the  petitioner  and
learned  counsel  appearing  for  the  respective  respondents/IIT,
Kharagpur and IIT, Roorkee.
8. Learned counsel for the IIT, Roorkee submitted that if this Court
is inclined to grant the relief to the petitioner, then he would have to
join  the  first  year/semester  of  B.Arch.  course  inasmuch  as  there
cannot be a continuity in the course on transfer. Secondly, the order
to be passed in this case may not be treated as a precedent insofar as
the IIT, Roorkee is concerned.
9. In response to this submission, learned senior counsel for the
petitioner  submitted  that  the  petitioner  is  willing  to  join  the  first
year/semester of B.Arch. course in the IIT, Roorkee as he is  availing
medical treatment from PGIMER, Chandigarh. In the circumstances,
this  Court  may  exercise  its  power  under  Article  142  of  the
Constitution of India and grant relief to the petitioner herein.
10. We find that the interest of justice would be served in the instant
case if a direction is issued to respondent no.1 to issue necessary
transfer/migration certificate and other original documents pertaining
to  the  petitioner  so  that  he  could  take  transfer/migration  and
admission in the IIT, Roorkee. The said exercise shall be carried out
5

--- Page 373 ---
within a period of one week from today as the current academic year is
stated to have commenced on 17.07.2026. The respondent IIT-Roorkee
shall admit the petitioner immediately on furnishing the migration
certificate as well as other relevant documents by the petitioner.
11. Ordered accordingly.
12. We have passed this order in exercise of our powers under Article
142 of the Constitution of India bearing in mind the peculiar health
issues faced by the petitioner herein and the fact that he is availing
treatment at Chandigarh whereas he is currently pursuing his studies
at IIT, Kharagpur and on account of the distance between the two
places his ailments have not been effectively treated.
13. It is needless to observe that the petitioner shall comply with all
the requirements regarding the fee structure and other payments that
the petitioner has to make to the IIT, Roorkee.
6

--- Page 374 ---
14. With  the  above observations  and directions, the Writ Petition
stands disposed.
Pending application(s) shall stand disposed of.
 …..………………....................J.
                                (B.V. NAGARATHNA)
  ……………….……………………J.
(R. MAHADEVAN)
 NEW DELHI
 JULY 30, 2026

IN THE SUPREME COURT OF INDIA
CIVIL APPELLATE JURISDICTION
CIVIL APPEAL NO.9915 OF 2026
(Arising out of S.L.P.(Civil) No.14733 of 2024)
K.V. RAMANACHARI  ... APPELLANT(S) 
                  VS.
MANAMMA & ORS.              ... RESPONDENT(S)
                                                         
          O R D E R
1. Leave granted.
2. Heard Ms. Bina Madhavan, learned counsel appearing
for the appellant.  The respondents, though served, have
chosen not to appear.
3. The present appeal has been filed challenging the
judgment and order dated 24 th June, 2024 passed by the
High Court for the State of Telangana at Hyderabad in
Contempt Appeal No.35 of 2015.
4. The grievance of the appellant is that in Contempt
Case No.1043 of 2015 by judgment dated 3rd December, 2015,
the learned Single Judge sentenced the appellant to two
months’  simple  imprisonment  and  fine  of  Rs.1,500/-
(Rupees one thousand and five hundred).  The contempt
itself arose since the respondents herein alleged non-
implementation and wilful disobedience of the order dated
1

--- Page 386 ---
30th January, 2025 passed by the learned Single Judge in
Writ Petition No.28857 of 2014.
5. By  the  said  order,  the  learned  Single  Judge
directed the Commissioner, Municipal Corporation as well
as the State Government to initiate proceedings under
Section  147  of  the  Greater  Hyderabad  Municipal
Corporation Act, 1955 in accordance with the provisions
of the  Right to Fair Compensation and Transparency in
Land Acquisition, Rehabilitation and Resettlement Act,
2013  for  acquisition  of  the  entire  land  of  the
respondents for “open space/park” and pay compensation to
the respondents herein.  It was further directed that the
requisition for the said purpose should be sent by the
appellant herein to the State of Telangana within a
period of two weeks from the date of receipt of copy of
the order and that the State of Telangana should initiate
the process for acquisition within a period of one month
thereafter and conclude the same within a period of three
months.
6. When notice was issued in the Contempt Petition, a
counter  affidavit  was  filed  by  the  appellant  herein
stating that a Writ Appeal SR No.76697 of 2015 had been
filed against the order passed in the Writ Petition with
an appropriate application for condonation of delay.  The
learned Single Judge found that mere pendency of the Writ
2

--- Page 387 ---
Appeal could not operate as a stay of the order passed in
the Writ Petition.  So holding the learned Single Judge
found wilful disobedience by the appellant of the order
dated 30th January, 2015 in Writ Petition No.28857 of 2014
and passed the order on sentence, as indicated above.
7. As pointed out above, a Writ Appeal had been filed
by the State against the order of the learned Single
Judge which was pending.  Questioning the order punishing
him for contempt,  the appellant filed Contempt Appeal
No.35 of 2015 under Section 19 of the Contempt of Courts
Act, 1971, wherein interim orders were passed staying the
operation of the sentence.  The Writ Appeal filed by the
State, namely, Writ Appeal No.1060 of 2015 (filed against
the main judgment of the learned Single Judge) and the
Contempt Appeal filed by the appellant being Contempt
Appeal No.35 of 2015 were taken up for hearing together.
8. By the impugned order, while upholding the judgment
of the learned Single Judge and dismissing the Writ
Appeal,  the  Division  Bench  without  any  discussion
whatsoever dismissed the Contempt Appeal filed by the
appellant in view of the dismissal of the Writ Appeal.
3

--- Page 388 ---
9. Being aggrieved, the appellant is before us.
10. Ms. Bina Madhavan, learned counsel appearing for
the  appellant  submits  that  when  the  Special  Leave
Petition filed by the appellant came up for hearing on
19th July, 2024, this Court stayed the impugned order
insofar as the directions with regard to the confirmation
of the sentence in contempt was concerned.  
11. Learned counsel also contends that there has been
no wilful disobedience on the part of the appellant.
Learned counsel also contends that while the learned
Single Judge order was passed on 30 th January, 2015, the
appellant had taken charge barely eleven days before.
The appellant, thereafter, was informed about the Writ
Appeal and he was under the  bona fide  impression that
since the Writ Appeal was pending at the behest of the
State, any action would have to await the outcome of the
Writ Appeal.  In the meantime, on 25 th April, 2015, the
Contempt Case came to be filed by the predecessors of the
respondents herein.
12. Learned counsel contends that there has been no
discussion whatsoever at all on the wilful nature of the
disobedience or otherwise, either in the order of the
learned Single Judge or in the order of the Division
Bench.
4

--- Page 389 ---
13. Learned counsel also brings an important subsequent
development. Pursuant to the impugned order on 10 th July,
2024, the respondents executed a Gift Deed of the land in
question to the Municipal Corporation and the Municipal
Corporation  on  20 th July,  2024  gave  Transferable
Development Right Certificate to the respondents for TDR
value of 1694 square yards (i.e. 423.50 square yards x
400%) at the land value of Rs.10,000/- per square yard.
No  wonder  that,  since  the  respondents  are  fully
satisfied, they are not appearing in spite of service.
14. The  only  question  before  us  is  whether  the
conviction  and  sentence  of  the  appellant  under  the
Contempt Of Courts Act was justified.  Though we are not
satisfied with the explanation given by the appellant
that he was lulled into inaction by the pendency of the
Writ Appeal, we are of the opinion that there is no
wilful disobedience of the order.  We say this on the
peculiar facts and circumstances of the present case.
The appellant had also only 11 days before the order of
the  learned  Single  Judge  taken  charge  as  Municipal
Commissioner.
5

--- Page 390 ---
15. Keeping all these facts and circumstances in mind,
we are of the opinion that the contempt action against
the appellant was not justified.  The Division Bench also
has not independently considered the statutory appeal
filed by the appellant against the sentence under the
Contempt of Courts Act.  After dismissing the Writ Appeal
on merits as a consequential order, the Contempt Appeal
has also been dismissed.
16. Be that as it may, we find that there is no wilful
disobedience on the part of the appellant. We set aside
the judgments of both the Division Bench dated 24 th June,
2024 in Contempt Appeal No.35 of 2015 as well as that of
the learned Single Judge dated 3 rd December, 2015 in
Contempt Case No.1043 of 2015.  The appellant will stand
acquitted of the charge of contempt.
17. The appeal is allowed in the above terms.
..........................J.
       (K.V.VISWANATHAN)
                          
 ..........................J.
       (ARUN PALLI) 
NEW DELHI;
July 31, 2026

1. Leave granted.
2. The  High  Court  of  Judicature  for  Rajasthan  at
Jodhpur, by the impugned judgment and order dated
13th May, 2026, has rejected the appellants’ prayers
for bail in anticipation of arrest. 
3. Appellants, figure as accused in FIR No.0289 of
Crl. Appeal @ SLP (Crl.) No.10705/2026 1

--- Page 400 ---
2024 dated 04 th December, 2024 registered at Police
Station Parbatsar, District Didwana Kuchaman under
Sections 121(1), 132, 351(2), 189(2) of the Bharatiya
Nyaya Sanhita (BNS), 2023 and Sections 3(1)(r), 3(1)
(s)  and  3(2)(va)  of  the  Scheduled  Caste  and
Scheduled T ribe (Prevention of Atrocities) Act, 1989. 
4. We  have  heard  learned  counsel  appearing  for
the  appellants  as  well  as  the  respondent-State  of
Rajasthan.
5. Learned counsel appearing for the respondent-
State  submits  that  counter-affidavit  has  been  filed
and he tenders a copy thereof. 
6. It  is  not  in  dispute  that  the  appellants  have
joined investigation in terms of the earlier order of
this Court.
7. Learned counsel for the respondent-State also
submits that charge-sheet has since been filed. 
8. Having  regard  to  the  nature  of  allegations
coupled  with  the  facts  that  the  appellants  have
Crl. Appeal @ SLP (Crl.) No.10705/2026 2

--- Page 401 ---
joined  investigation  and the  chargesheet  has  also
been filed, we  are  of the  considered opinion  that
their  detention  for  custodial  interrogation  is  no
longer necessary and that they may be admitted to
an order for grant of bail in anticipation of arrest.
9. We,  accordingly,  set  aside  the  judgment  and
order impugned in this appeal.

11. Needless  to  observe,  the  appellants  shall  not,
directly or indirectly, by making inducement, threat
or promise, dissuade any person acquainted with the
facts of the case from disclosing such facts to any
police officer or to the court.
12. We  clarify  that  the  observations  made  in  this
order  and  grant  of  bail  to  the  appellants  in

 IN THE SUPREME COURT OF INDIA
CRIMINAL APPELLATE JURISDICTION
CRIMINAL APPEAL  NO.         OF 2026
(@ Special Leave Petition (Crl.) No.11298/2026)
MAJID HUSSAIN & ANR.      ...APPELLANT(S) 
                                VERSUS
STATE OF U.P                    ….RESPONDENT(S)
O R D E R
Leave granted.
This criminal appeal challenges the order dated
05.03.2025 passed by the High Court of Judicature at
Allahabad in Criminal Appeal No. 12339 of 2024, whereby
the appellants’ application for suspension of sentence
was dismissed.
The appellants faced trial in connection with
FIR No. 525/2018 dated 16.08.2018 registered at Police
Station Ramgarh, District Firozabad. By judgment dated
25.11.2024,  the  Additional  District  and  Sessions
Judge/Fast Track Court No.2, Firozabad (‘Trial Court’)
convicted the appellants under Sections 304B, 498A and
1

--- Page 412 ---
323/34 of the Indian Penal Code, 1860 (‘IPC’) and
Sections  3/4  of  the  Dowry  Prohibition  Act,  1961
(‘DPA’). 
By order of sentence dated 25.11.2024 passed by
the Trial Court, the appellants were sentenced to ten
years’  rigorous  imprisonment  for  the  offence  under
Section  304B  of  the  IPC,  two  years’  rigorous
imprisonment and a fine of Rs.2,000/- for the offence
under  Section  498A  IPC,  two  years’  rigorous
imprisonment and a fine of Rs. 1,000/- for the offence
under Sections 3/4 of the DPA, and six months’ rigorous
imprisonment and fine of Rs. 500/- for the offence
under Sections 323/34 of the IPC. The sentences were
directed to run concurrently. 
The appellants, being aggrieved by the judgment and
order passed by the Trial Court, filed Criminal Appeal
No. 12339 of 2024 before the High Court of Judicature
at Allahabad and the same is pending. The appellants
also preferred application for suspension of sentence
during the pendency of the appeal.  
The  High  Court,  by  the  impugned  order  dated
05.03.2025, dismissed the application for suspension of
sentence. Hence, the present criminal appeal.
2

--- Page 413 ---
By order dated 08.06.2026, this Court issued
notice in the instant matter. 
We have heard learned counsel for the appellants
and learned counsel for the State and perused the
material on record.
Learned counsel for the appellants submitted
that the sentence imposed upon the appellants by the
Sessions Court is ten years of rigorous imprisonment.
Appellant No.1 has completed six years and nine months
while appellant no.2 has completed seven years and ten
months  imprisonment  out  of  ten  years  imprisonment.
Their application seeking suspension of sentence  was
dismissed by the High Court.  Their appeal before the
High Court is of the year 2024. The hearing of the
appeal by the High Court would inevitably be delayed
having regard to the fact that the appeals of the
earlier years are being heard.  In the circumstances,
the High Court ought to have granted suspension of
sentence and bail to the appellants herein.  Further,
the appellants are having good case on merits and if
the relief is not granted to them at this stage, the
appellants would inevitably complete their sentence and
in case they are acquitted in the case, it would be of
no   avail   to   them.  He  further submitted that the
3

--- Page 414 ---
impugned order may be set aside and the relief of
suspension of sentence and bail may be granted to the
appellants.
Per contra,  learned counsel appearing for the
respondent/State submitted that there is no merit in
the appeal and the same may be dismissed.
Considering the facts on record, in our view,
the case for suspension of sentence is made out. We
therefore direct as follows:
“The appellants shall be produced before the
concerned Trial Court as early as possible and
the Trial Court shall release them on bail,
subject to  such conditions  as it  may deem
appropriate to impose to ensure their presence
in the proceedings in Criminal Appeal No. 12339
of 2024 mentioned above.”
The appellants shall appear before the High Court
as and when directed to do so.
It is directed that the appellants shall extend
complete cooperation in the hearing of the appeal
before the High Court. The appellants shall not misuse
their liberty in any manner.
4

--- Page 415 ---
Any infraction of the conditions may entail  
cancellation of the suspension of sentence granted 
to the appellants.
With these observations, the criminal appeal is 
allowed.
      ………………………………………J.
  [B.V. NAGARATHNA]
….……………………………………J.
       [R. MAHADEVAN]

O R D E R
1. Leave granted.
2. Misplaced sympathy of the Court may itself result in injustice
by rewarding a wholly undeserving litigant. The appeals on
hand stand as testimony to this.
3. The appellant, N.R. Mani, is the plaintiff in O.S. No. 50 of
2010 on the file of the learned Principal District Judge,
Karur, which was filed by him for recovery of a sum of
11,58,650/- (Rupees eleven lakhs fifty eight thousand six₹
hundred fifty only) from the respondent, S.P. Sivakumar, the
defendant therein.  Parties shall, hereinafter, be referred to
as arrayed in the suit.
4. The record reflects that the defendant entered appearance
before the trial Court through counsel and filed his written
statement  on  09/10.11.2010.  Upon  framing  of  issues,  the
plaintiff  examined  himself  as  PW-1  and  the  matter  was
1

--- Page 418 ---
adjourned to 21/22.11.2011 to enable his cross-examination by
the defendant.  However, there was no representation for the
defendant on that day.  He was, accordingly, set ex parte and
the suit was decreed. The defendant filed an application under
Order IX Rule 13 of the Code of Civil Procedure, 1908 1, on
15.12.2011.  As the said application was filed without giving
notice to the plaintiff, it was returned on 02.02.2012 with a
direction to serve notice upon the other side.  Notice was
thereupon served upon the plaintiff on 28.04.2016, that is,
four years later. The application was returned on 29.07.2016
and though it was re-presented on the same date, it was again
returned on 01.09.2016. 
5. Thereafter, the defendant chose to sleep over the matter for a
few more years. He filed a condone delay application so as to
maintain his application for setting aside the decree only on
16.10.2020.  Significant to note, on the strength of the ex
parte  decree  passed  in  his  favour,  the  plaintiff  had
instituted  execution  proceedings  in  E.P.  No.  61/2020  on
20.09.2020. The defendant chose to act only thereafter. As
stated earlier, an application was filed by him on 16.10.2020
in I.A. No. 1 of 2020 in O.S. No. 50 of 2010, praying for
condonation of the delay of 2973 days in the filing of the
application under Order IX Rule 13 of the CPC.
6. Having considered the said application in the light of the
aforestated  facts,  the  learned  Principal  District  Judge,
1  “CPC”, for short
2

--- Page 419 ---
Karur, dismissed the application by a detailed order on
26.08.2022. Simultaneously, in Execution Petition No. 61 of
2020, an order was passed on 26.08.2022, directing attachment
of the property of the defendant.  
7. Civil Revision Petition (MD) Nos. 2021 of 2022 and 2047 of
2022 were filed against these orders by the defendant. These
revisions came to be allowed by a learned Judge of the High
Court of Judicature at Madras, vide the common impugned order
dated 30.07.2025.
8. Perusal of the said order reflects that the learned Judge was
inclined to take a lenient view as the defendant offered to
deposit 5,00,000/- (Rupees five lakhs only) in addition to₹
the  sum  of  2,00,000/-  (Rupees  two  lakhs  only)  already₹
deposited by him, as per an earlier order.
9. Accepting this belated attempt on the part of the defendant to
demonstrate  his  purported  bonafides,  the  learned  Judge
directed the deposit of a further sum of 5,00,000/- (Rupees₹
five lakhs only) to be made within two weeks. Subject thereto,
the learned Judge restored the suit and directed the trial
Court to allow the parties to contest the same and then pass
appropriate orders on merits and in accordance with law within
six months. The order of attachment passed in the execution
proceedings was, in consequence, set aside.
10. Aggrieved by the largesse extended to the defendant, the
plaintiff approached this Court.  Further proceedings in O.S.
No. 50 of 2010 were stayed by this Court on 27.10.2025.
3

--- Page 420 ---
11. This being the narrative, the defendant chose to file a
counter affidavit before this Court, wherein he chose to
completely ignore the facts on record and boldly stated in
paragraph 3 thereof that he only became aware of the existence
of the decree upon the initiation of execution proceedings in
2020. To augment this clear display of his lack of bonafides,
he then stated that the delay in the filing of an application
to set aside the ex parte decree was neither intentional nor a
result of gross negligence, but was a direct consequence of
the lack of knowledge of the proceedings initiated behind his
back.
12. This blatant disregard for the truth and the resort to
falsehoods by the defendant clearly manifests that the High
Court was not justified in showing him any sympathy or
leniency.  A litigant, who sleeps over an  ex parte  decree
passed as long back as on 22.11.2011 for nearly nine years and
then takes recourse to an application for condonation of
lengthy delay only after institution of execution proceedings
against him, is not entitled to any compassion.
13. The undeserved indulgence extended to the defendant by way of
the common order under appeal, therefore, cannot be sustained,
be it on facts or in law.
14. The appeals are accordingly allowed, setting aside the common
order dated 30.07.2025. The orders passed on 26.08.2022,
dismissing  the  condone  delay  application  and  directing
attachment of the defendant’s property, shall stand restored.
4

--- Page 421 ---
The parties shall bear their own costs.
Pending application(s), if any, stand disposed of.

          UPON hearing the counsel the Court made the following
                             O R D E R
1. Pursuant  to  our  order  dated  22.05.2026,
Master Garvit (i.e., the ward) has been admitted
1

--- Page 440 ---
in Class VI of a boarding school, named Duhan
Public  School,  Rohtak,  with  effect  from
01.07.2026.
2. We interacted with Garvit today. He appears
more confident. It seems his admission in a
boarding  school  leading  to  interaction  with
fellow students and staff of the institution has
helped in increasing his overall confidence.
3. However,  the  respondent  has  applied  for
guidelines on the weekend custody of Garvit. It
is alleged in the application that as per the
policy of the boarding school, the child can go
to  his  parents’  or  guardian’s  place  once  a
month. It is stated that the petitioner had
taken weekend custody of Garvit twice in a month
i.e., on 4 th/5th July 2026 and 12 th  July 2026. It
has been submitted that if Garvit continues to
be in continuous touch with the petitioner, then
possibility of him being tutored against his
father i.e., respondent cannot be ruled out.
4. In response to the above submission, on
behalf of the petitioner, it has been submitted
that 5 th  July 2026 was Garvit’s birthday and,
therefore,  he  wanted  to  go  to  his  maternal
2

--- Page 441 ---
grandfather’s place; whereas, on 12 th July 2026,
Garvit  wanted  to  collect  his  books  etc.  to
prepare a project assigned to him, therefore he
came over. The petitioner, however, undertakes
that he would not violate the policy of the
boarding school.
5. At this stage, the learned counsel for the
respondent submitted that since the policy of
the boarding school allows the child to go once
a month to his parents’/guardians’ place, it
would  be  appropriate  that  this  Court  may
regulate the monthly weekend custody of Garvit.
6. In response, on behalf of the petitioner, it
has been submitted that monthly weekend custody
of  Garvit  should  be  alternated  between
petitioner and respondent, that is, if weekend
custody of Garvit for August is with the father,
the following month’s weekend custody of Garvit
should be with the maternal grandfather.
7. We accept the above suggestion. Accordingly,
we direct as follows:
(i). Both sides shall strictly follow
the discipline of the boarding school which
allows child to be with parents/ guardian
3

--- Page 442 ---
only once a month and not more;
(ii) The weekend custody of Garvit, as per
the policy of the boarding school, for the
month of August 2026 shall be with the
father i.e., the respondent.  To ensure that
there is no dispute regarding the week in
which custody of Garvit is to be provided
to  either  his  father  or  maternal
grandfather, we direct that weekend custody
of Garvit shall be with either his father
or maternal grandfather dependent on the
month, in the third week of the month. For
example, in the third week of August 2026
it shall be with the father (i.e., the
respondent). In the following month, that
is in the third week of September 2026,
weekend custody of Garvit shall be with his
maternal  grandfather.  Likewise,  this
alternating  custody  arrangement,  shall
continue  month  to  month  until  further
orders; 
(iii)  If any of the two parties has any
reservation on, or any issue regarding,
taking of weekend custody of Garvit, he
4

--- Page 443 ---
would inform the other side about it in
advance. In that event, the other party
shall have a right to accept the weekend
custody of Garvit for that month. 
(iv) For the sake of convenience and safety
of the child, we direct the parties to
share  their  mobile  number(s),  their
addresses as also the place where the child
would be put over the weekend when custody

1. Heard.
2. Leave granted.
3. Appellant  who  has  been  arraigned  as  an  accused  in  FIR  No.
153/2025 for the offences punishable under Sections 316, 318 and
Section  61(2)  of  Bharatiya  Nyaya  Sanhita,  2023  (BNS)  had
approached the Sessions Court for grant of anticipatory bail and by
order  dated  09.07.2025,  the  said  prayer  was  granted  subject  to
several conditions. One of the conditions imposed was :
 “f) The petitioner shall report before the Investigating
Officer on the first and third Saturday of every calendar
month between 10.00 AM and 12.00 noon, till the charge
sheet is filed.”
1                                                                         SLP(CRL.) NO.14227 OF 2025

--- Page 450 ---
4. The said condition having been violated resulted in an application
for cancellation of bail was filed and the jurisdictional High Court by
the  impugned  order  dated  25.02.2026  cancelled  the  same,  after
noticing that appellant himself had filed a criminal miscellaneous
application for relaxation of one of the conditions and same had
been allowed and nothing prevented the appellant to seek relaxation
of the condition no. F  (supra) also. On account of not adhering to the
said condition, the bail granted by the Sessions Court, came to be
cancelled by the impugned order.
5. This Court while ordering notice on 13.04.2026 had granted an
interim protection to the effect that no coercive steps shall be taken
against the appellant. Even prior to that during the pendency of the
proceedings before the High Court, the appellant has appeared on
06.02.2026  and  08.02.2026  before  the  Investigating  Officer  (IO)
pursuant to the notice dated 31.01.2026 issued by IO.
6. As  such,  we  are  of  the  considered  view  that  the  order  of
cancellation  of  bail  need  not  be  sustained  particularly  in  the
background  of  learned  counsel  appearing  for  the  appellant  also
undertaking to comply with the condition no.F (supra) in letter and
spirit and also undertaking that there would be no infraction of this
condition. Hence, impugned order is set aside and order granting the
bail  passed  by  Sessions  Court  is  restored.  Though  the  learned
counsel appearing for the appellant prays for relaxation of the said
condition, we are not inclined to entertain this prayer and it is open
to  the  appellant  to  apply  before  the  jurisdictional  court  for  the
relaxation of the said condition, if so advised.
2                                                                         SLP(CRL.) NO.14227 OF 2025

--- Page 451 ---
7. It is made clear that until and unless any order relaxing the said
condition is passed, the appellant shall continue to appear before the
IO as per condition no.F(supra).
8. Accordingly, the appeal is allowed. Impugned order is set aside.

One male child was born to the petitioner and the respondent from

the court of Civil Judge, Senior Division Gondia, Maharashtra,  which
is  at  a  distance  of  around  200  kms  from  her  present  place  of
residence, that interest of justice demands grant of the prayer for
transfer. That apart, vide this Court’s order dated 13th October, 2025,
other proceedings  also stand transferred and are pending in the

Court,  Raipur  in  Chhattisgarh. Records  of  H.M.P.  No.7/2025  be
transferred to the transferee court immediately.

transferee court on 20 th August, 2026. If any or both the parties fail

will fix another date of appearance. Thereafter, he shall be free to
proceed in accordance with law.
10. Notwithstanding that mediation has failed, the presiding officer
of the transferee court shall endeavour to bring about a settlement
between the parties through the process of mediation. If the process

--- Page 461 ---

the  proceedings  to  its  logical  conclusion  on  its  merits  and  in

on any occasion, he will be at liberty to seek permission to attend

to A-3. This essentially resulted in rejection of the appellant’s prayer for
quashing of criminal proceedings.
5. A-2 having since passed away during the process of investigation,
chargesheet was not filed against him. 
6. At the time of entertaining the special leave petition 2, out of which
this criminal appeal arises, this Court had dismissed the plea of the
1  FIR No.30/2023 dated 22nd September, 2023 under Sections 498A, 504, 506 and 34, 
Indian Penal Code
2  SLP (Crl.) No.7763/2025
1

--- Page 470 ---
husband of the respondent no.2 being the petitioner no.1 and issued
notice on the plea of the appellant.
7. We have heard Ms. Kaveeta Walia, learned senior counsel for the
appellant, Mr. D. K. Thakur, learned counsel for the respondent no.1-
State as well as Ms. Neha Malik, learned counsel for the respondent
no.2.
8. Decisions of this Court in  Dara Lakshmi Narayana and Others
Vs. State of Telangana & Another 3 and  Digambar and Another
Vs. State of Maharashtra and Anr. 4 have been referred to by Ms.
Walia in support of her contention that the proceedings  against the
appellant ought to be quashed.
9. Ms.  Malik,  however,  contends  that  the  High  Court  was  right  in
observing, having regard to the nature of offence alleged to have been
committed by the appellant, that a mini-trial cannot be held at the stage
of considering a quashing petition and that she ought to stand trial. 
10. Having noted the contents of the FIR and the chargesheet 5 that has
since been filed, we find that the allegations levelled by the respondent
no.2 against the appellant are vague, indefinite and omnibus. Not a
single  specific  incident  with  particulars  of  date  and  time,  when  the
appellant treated the respondent no.2 with cruelty, has been referred to
in the complaint. Significantly, it is admitted by the respondent no.2 that
she and the appellant, who is married since 2015, did not share the
same roof.   
3  (2025) 3 SCC 735 (Paras 26, 27 and 34)
4  2024 SCC Online 3836
5  C.S. No.30/23 dated 10th October, 2023 under Sections 498A, 504, 506 and 34, Indian 
Penal Code
2

--- Page 471 ---
11. As has rightly been submitted by Ms. Walia, the appellant may not
have lived up to the expectations of the respondent no.2 as a dutiful
sister-in-law by attending to her during her pregnancy but that by itself
cannot and does not amount to a criminal offence for which she should
be made to stand trial.
12. Consequently,  proceedings  against  the  appellant  shall  stand
quashed.
13. The appeal is, accordingly, allowed on the aforesaid terms.
14. Pending application(s), if any, stand disposed of.

JYOTI SONI                        Appellant(s)

O R D E R
Leave granted.
The appellant being a lady, seeks bail in
connection with FIR No.296/2025, dated 05.10.2025,
registered at Police Station: Parasia, District –
Chhindwara  for  the  offences  punishable  under
Sections  105  and  276  of  the  Bharatiya  Nyaya
Sanhita, 2023, and Section 27A of the Drugs and
Cosmetics Act, 1940.
We have heard the learned counsel appearing
for the parties.
The appellant before us, runs a pharmacy and
is  not  the  manufacturer  of  the  cough  syrup.
Unfortunately, the cough syrup secured from the

--- Page 475 ---
2
appellant led to the death of so many innocent
victims.
Learned  Senior  Counsel  appearing  for  the
appellant submits that apart from the fact that
the co-accused has been granted bail and that the
appellant is a lady, it is nobody’s case that she
is the manufacturer of the cough syrup which
caused the deaths. Even assuming that she sold a
cough syrup other than the one prescribed, it is a
bona fide act, and not a criminal one. In view of
the above, the continued incarceration of the
appellant is not required.
Learned  counsel  appearing  for  the  State
submits  that  considering  the  consequences
involved, there is no need to interfere with the
impugned order.
We are inclined to set aside the impugned
order, and grant bail only for the reason that the
appellant, not only being a lady, but is only the
owner of the pharmacy.
Though  the  occurrence  is  unfortunate,

--- Page 476 ---
3
considering the facts governing, we are inclined
to hold that the appellant is certainly entitled
to the benefit of enlargement on bail.
Accordingly, the impugned order stands set
aside, and the appellant is granted bail on terms
and conditions to the satisfaction of the Trial
Court.
However, we make it clear that this order
will not enure to the benefit of the husband of
the appellant who is also an accused, and whose
application shall be decided on its own merits.
The appeal stands allowed, accordingly.
Pending application(s), if any, shall stand
disposed of.

2
          UPON hearing the counsel the Court made the following
                             O R D E R
1. The present petition filed by the guardian of a minor
victim calls in question the correctness of the order dated
dated  19-02-2026  in  Criminal  Misc.Bail  Application
No.44606/2025  passed  by  the  High  Court  of  Judicature  at
Allahabad. By the said order, the accused-respondent no.2
(Devendra Kumar Kushwaha) has been granted bail by the High
Court.
2. The brief facts of the case is that, an FIR was lodged
against respondent no.2 bearing No.923/2025 dated 05.10.2025
registered with Kotwali Police Station, District Deoria, Uttar
Pradesh, for the offences punishable under Sections 65(2),
115(2) & 351(2) of Bharatiya Nyaya Sanhita, 2023 (for short,
‘BNS’) and under Sections  5 and 6 of the  Protection of
Children from Sexual Offences Act, 2012 (for short, ‘POCSO’).
The respondent no.2 was arrested no 06.10.2025..
3. The gist of the prosecution’s case is that the victim was
a student of class VIII in ‘The Kids Valley School’, where it
is not disputed that respondent no.2 was the director. In
short the case of the prosecution as is available in the FIR
as well as the statement under Section 180 and 183 of the
Bharatiya Nagarik Suraksha Sanhita, 2023 of the prosecutrix is
that  she  was  subjected  to  repeated  sexual  assault  by
respondent no.2.  It was alleged that from July 2024 to June
2025 there were multiple instances of sexual assault. The
prosecution’s claim is that victim is 12 years old. The Trial

--- Page 515 ---
3
Judge has declined the bail to respondent no.2 after referring
to  the  facts  of  the  case  and  the  medical  records.  The
respondent no.2 moved the High Court. The High Court has, in
our opinion, not adverted to any of the basic consideration
which are required to be gone into in a bail application
especially in the case of a heinous offence. All of that the
learned counsel for the respondent no.2 could do was draw
attention to paragraph 10 of the impugned order which reads as
follows:-
“Considering the facts and circumstances of the case,
submissions made by learned counsel for the parties,
nature of offence, severity of punishment, delay in
lodging the FIR and also considering the attendance
sheet of the victim which indicates that on the date
of offence, victim was absent, prima facie I find it a
fit case to release the applicant on bail. The bail
application is allowed.”
4. We are not satisfied with the manner of disposal to the
bail application by the High Court. Facts in its barest
essentials which are required to be adverted to, do not find
mention. We are not discussing the facts in detail, lest it
prejudice the case of the respondent no.2, considering the
course of action that we propose to adopt.
5. For the reasons stated above, while setting aside the
impugned  order  dated  19-02-2026.  We  remit  the  Criminal
Misc.Bail Application No.44606/2025 for fresh consideration by
the High Court.
6. However, we direct that respondent no.2 shall surrender

--- Page 516 ---
4
before the concerned Trial Court within a period of three
weeks from today i.e. on or before 24.08.2026 and the Trial
Court shall take him into judicial custody.
7. After the respondent no.2 surrender, the High Court may
consider the bail application afresh uninfluenced by any of
the observations made in this order.

IN THE SUPREME COURT OF INDIA
CRIMINAL APPELLATE JURISDICTION
CRIMINAL APPEAL NO.   3569   OF 2026
(@ SPECIAL LEAVE PETITION (CRIMINAL) NO. 10569/2026)
KIRANPAL SINGH      APPELLANT(S)
VERSUS
STATE OF MADHYA PRADESH     RESPONDENT(S)
ORDER
1. We have heard learned counsel for the appellant and
learned  counsel  for  the  respondent-State  of  Madhya
Pradesh.
2. Leave granted.
3. Appellant is aggrieved by order dated 08.01.2026
passed by the High Court of Madhya Pradesh at Gwalior
(briefly the ‘High Court’ hereinafter), rejecting the
regular bail application of the appellant.
4. Appellant  is  an  accused  in  Crime  No.162/2023
registered at Police Station- Godan, District- Datia,
Madhya Pradesh under Sections 457, 380, 328 and 392 of
the Indian Penal Code,  1860 (for short, ‘IPC’) read
with Sections 11/13 of the MP Dakiti Aur Vyapharan
Prabhavit  Kshe tra  Adhiniyam,  1981.  Subsequently,
Sections 8/21 of the  Narcotic Drugs and Psychotropic
1

--- Page 530 ---
Substances Act, 1985 (for short, ‘NDPS Act’) have been
added.
5. Allegation against the appellant is that he is
involved in the theft of idols from a temple.
6. Learned counsel for the appellant submits that
appellant has been in custody since 28.11.2023, for
almost three years now. The investigation is complete,
whereafter  trial  has  commenced.  Therefore,  at  this
stage, continued detention of the appellant may not be
necessary.
7. Refuting the submission of learned counsel for the
appellant, learned counsel for the respondent-State of
Madhya Pradesh submits that appellant has a history of
committing similar offences. That apart, the trial is
proceeding expeditiously. Therefore, appellant may not
be enlarged on bail.
8. Having regard to the fact that appellant is in
custody  since  28.11.2023  with  the  investigation
complete and the trial having commenced, we are of the
view that further detention of the appellant would not
be justified.
9. Having regard to the above,  t he impugned order
dated 08.01.2026 passed by the High Court is set aside.
10. Consequently, we direct that the appellant shall be
produced  before  the  concerned  Judicial  Magistrate
2

--- Page 531 ---
within  a  maximum  period  of  07  days  from  today,
whereafter he shall be released on bail on such terms
and conditions as may be deemed appropriate.
11. Accordingly, the Criminal Appeal is allowed.
12. Pending  application(s),  if  any,  shall  stand
disposed of.

IN THE SUPREME COURT OF INDIA
CRIMINAL APPELLATE JURISDICTION
CRIMINAL APPEAL NO. 3570     OF 2026
(@ SPECIAL LEAVE PETITION (CRIMINAL) NO. 10701/2026)
ROY @ RONI JOSEF FERNANDIS      APPELLANT(S)
VERSUS
THE STATE OF MAHARASHTRA     RESPONDENT(S)
ORDER
1. We have heard learned counsel for the appellant and
learned  counsel  for  the  respondent-State  of
Maharashtra.
2. Leave granted.
3. Appellant is aggrieved by order dated 30.04.2026
passed by the High Court of Bombay (briefly the ‘High
Court’  hereinafter),  rejecting  the  regular  bail
application of the appellant.
4. Appellant  is  an  accused  in  CR  No.115/2025
registered  at  Police  Station-  Palghar,  District-
Palghar,  Maharashtra  under  Sections  309(6),  305,
331(4), 331(7) and 3(5) of the Bharatiya Nyaya Sanhita,
2023 (for short, ‘BNS’).
5. Allegation against the appellant is that of house
breaking  and  committing  theft.  Materials  on  record
1

--- Page 534 ---
discloses that appellant was allegedly apprehended at
the time of committing the offence.
6. Learned counsel for the appellant submits that
appellant is in custody for more than one year now. At
the time of his apprehension, he was subjected to
physical assault for which he has suffered grievous
injury. Investigation is complete, whereafter charge
sheet has been filed.
7. Learned  counsel  for  the  respondent-State  of
Maharashtra submits that appellant is a repeat offender
and  has  number  of  criminal  antecedents  of  similar
nature.  Therefore,  this  Court  may  not  enlarge  the
appellant  on  bail.  In  fact,  the  High  Court  has
requested the Trial Court to expedite the trial.
8. After hearing learned counsel for the parties, we
are of the view that appellant deserves to be enlarged
on bail, having regard to the nature of the offence and
the period of detention undergone.
9. Accordingly, t he impugned order dated 30.04.2026
passed by the High Court is set aside.
10. Consequently, we direct that the appellant shall be
produced before the Trial Court within a maximum period
of 07 days from today, whereafter he shall be released
on bail on such terms and conditions as may be deemed
appropriate.

--- Page 535 ---
11. Accordingly, the Criminal Appeal is allowed.
12. Pending  application(s),  if  any,  shall  stand
disposed of.

and  order  dated  23rd February,  2006  passed  by  the  High  Court  of
Karnataka at Bangalore in Criminal Appeal No.1187 of 1999, whereby the
High Court has dismissed  the Criminal Appeal filed by the appellants
herein. 
2. The  relevant  facts of  the  present  case  are  that  four  accused  were
charge sheeted for committing offences punishable under Sections 302,
201 read with Section 34 of the Indian Penal Code, 1860 1, for committing
the murder of the deceased Chandrakant. While accused nos. 1 to 3 are
brothers; accused no.4 is the wife of the deceased and sister of accused
nos. 1 to 3.
1  For short the ‘IPC’
1

--- Page 542 ---
3. The case of the prosecution is that as the deceased was harassing and
inflicting  cruelty  on  his  wife  (accused  no.4),  accused  persons  on  19th
March, 1994 at about 9.00 p.m., severely assaulted the deceased-brother-
in-law in his house and caused his death. According to the chargesheet, the
accused later on threw the body of the deceased in Bhima river to make
the evidence disappear.
4. The  Trial  Court  acquitted  the  accused-wife  (Accused  no.4),  but
convicted accused nos. 1 to 3 under Section 326 read with Section 34 of
the IPC and sentenced them to rigorous imprisonment for ten years. 
5. Though, the High Court by the impugned judgment held that the Trial
Court has blundered in appreciating the evidence of eye-witnesses, PW1
(Shreesail)  and  PW8  (Shayamrao)  and  the  medical  evidence  and  not
holding the accused guilty under Section 302 of the IPC, yet the High
Court confirmed the order of the Trial Court on the ground that a Court in
Appeal cannot impose a higher sentence in absence of the appeal by the
State.
6. This Court while issuing notice on 30 th July, 2007 had also issued
notice to the appellants-accused as to why their conviction under Section
326 of the IPC be not altered to one under Section 302 of the IPC.
7. During  the  pendency  of  the  present  appeal,  the  appellant  no.1
(Accused  no.1)  has  unfortunately  passed  away  and  consequently,  the
appeal has abated against him.
2

--- Page 543 ---
8. Learned Senior Counsel for the appellants states that the High Court
has erred in holding that the accused are guilty of offences punishable
under Section 326 read with Section 34 of the IPC without assigning any
reason and without any reference to any material on record. He further
states that the Courts below erred in relying upon the testimony of PW1,
who  is  the  cousin  brother  of  the  deceased,  even  when  PW8,  another
eyewitness does not mention about the presence of PW1 at the time of the
incident. He further states that the motive alleged is highly improbable for
causing commission of offence by the appellants.
9. Learned AAG for the respondent-State of Karnataka contends that the
impugned judgment of the High Court is well considered and calls for no
interference. He has taken us through the evidence of PW1 and PW8 to
contend that the ocular evidence and medical evidence establishes beyond
doubt that the present case falls in the 3 rd category of Section 300 of the
IPC. 
10. Having  heard  learned  counsel  for  the  parties  and  examining  the
material on record, this Court is of the view that the testimonies of PW1
and PW8 do not corroborate each other and cannot be relied upon. It is
pertinent  to  mention  that  both  PW1  and  PW8  state  that  they  were
eyewitnesses to the incident of murder, yet in their testimonies they do not
acknowledge the presence of each other.
3

--- Page 544 ---
11. Since, in the present case this Court has doubt about the presence of
the  eyewitnesses,  namely,  PW1  and  PW8,  the  appellants-accused  are
entitled to benefit of doubt. It is settled law that mere suspicion, however
strong or probable it may be, is no effective substitute for legal proof.
12.  Accordingly, the impugned judgment is set aside and the appellants
are given benefit of doubt and are acquitted of the charges framed against
them. They are on bail. Their bail bonds stand discharged.
13.  The Criminal Appeal stands disposed of with the above observations
and directions.
14.  Pending application(s), if any, shall stand disposed of.

(MANMOHAN)
